decision: KEEP TypeScript/native abort and timer APIs; FIX timer-side cancellation and terminal callback retirement.
constraints: One read-only session in Node or a browser host, synchronous display callbacks, native Fetch streams and an existing 20 ms requested expiry timer.
Abort state must withdraw aggregate details at the next rendering opportunity even before a pending read reaction; terminal callbacks must become inert before remote deletion settles.
Preserve public types, fixed transport errors, independent best-effort DELETE, and frozen timing/byte limits; add no replay queue or credential storage.

alternatives.technology: TypeScript with native AbortSignal and scoped rendering flag
alternatives.assessment: Selected: inspect the combined native abort state before rendering and retire the closure in finally. Direct host interoperation and static types express this small single-session lifetime without extra runtime ownership machinery. Six focused cases and bundled parity exercise the behavior.

Supports the same closure and native abort-state check. Erasing TypeScript syntax does not change runtime cancellation or supply a stronger boundary; no material advantage for the typed consumer API was established.

The tagged 7.8.2 source closes a subscription before finalizers and supports parent/child resource grouping. That is useful for a graph of reactive resources. This single Fetch reader and timer still need explicit signal-to-display withdrawal; introducing subscription ownership does not remove the demonstrated gate and adds a runtime abstraction without a required resource graph.

Official documentation describes transpilation to JavaScript and ESM interoperation plus JVM/mobile code sharing. This host boundary has no current cross-platform shared implementation requirement. It still needs host abort-state and callback-lifetime handling; no correctness or deployment win over a direct typed ESM API is established.

The official Fetch example uses host Request/Response and JsFuture. This component has no native computation kernel or memory-isolation requirement that a Wasm module would satisfy; host callbacks and cancellation still need explicit integration. No measured native performance advantage is claimed.

limits: Abort-state checking happens when the timer callback executes; it does not synchronously erase an already delivered copy or preempt a running callback.
Retained-callback injection checks the application lifetime guard; it does not assert that a conforming native timer invokes a cleared callback.
Native HTTP testing runs on Node loopback. Browser timing/accessibility, actual hardware latency and independent installed-product acceptance remain unqualified.
No cross-language speed benchmark was performed. The choice follows host API and single-session ownership constraints, not installed-tool convenience.
No additional runtime dependency, changed API contract, real actuation, targeting, surveillance history or availability/security certification.
